paper_title: Beyond Watching and Searching: Benchmarking Agents for Video-centered Deep Research Reports

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Deep research agents synthesize open-web evidence into long reports, but current benchmarks do not evaluate research centered on a source video. We introduce Video-Centered Deep Research Report Generation. Given a video and user request, an agent identifies research questions, retrieves external multimodal evidence, and produces an interactive report linked to relevant video moments. This task has direct practical value because it helps users locate relevant moments, verify claims, reproduce demonstrated procedures, and make informed decisions from video content. We present a skill-based workflow and OmniDR-Bench for this task. For evaluation, we propose Omni Atomic Rubric Trees (Omni-ARTs). Each tree contains three dimensions, 23 shared directions, and task-specific atomic binary criteria. The directions test audiovisual grounding, multimodal evidence use, and interactive presentation. Audited Rubric Construction (ARC) builds these trees through independent evidence collection, automated checks, behavioral calibration, and iterative human review. OmniDR-Bench contains 50 Chinese and English tasks across 19 realworld subcategories. It includes 6,414 criteria. Across 18 agent configurations, the best system scores 63.3 out of 100. Current agents still need broader content coverage, stronger causal and logical analysis across modalities, and more accurate citation support. We further analyze models, harnesses, skill configurations, video categories, and research trajectories. The code and data are released at https://github.com/marinero4972/OmniDR-Bench.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Videos teach knowledge, share opinions, demonstrate procedures, and advertise products through speech, imagery, and temporal context. Compared with text, video natively preserves richer situational context, visible entities, spatial relations, and fine-grained actions that are difficult to verbalize completely. These cues can reveal questions about mechanisms, credibility, alternatives, and practical use that broad text topic may not expose. Viewers may therefore need to locate relevant moments, verify claims and background, discover related material, or apply the content to real decision. These needs call for research that remains centered on the source video. Existing agents address only parts of this goal. Text-centered deep research agents produce cited reports through iterative web search and synthesis (Java et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025; Qiao et al., 2025). They do not require the audiovisual or temporal evidence of given video. Video deep research combines source-video evidence with open-web retrieval and multi-step reasoning (Liang et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026a; Gao et al., 2026; Fang et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026b; Zhang et al., 2026b). Its benchmarks mainly target difficult question answering (QA) tasks with short answers. Text-image research report systems (Shi et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026a; Ma et al., 2026) synthesize multimodal web material without taking source video or retrieved videos as research evidence. No existing setting evaluates complete research report that is organized around one source video and enriched by external multimodal evidence. We introduce Video-Centered Deep Research Report Generation to fill this gap. Given source video and user request, an agent identifies research-worthy claims, procedures, parameters, entities, and open questions. It investigates webpages, documents, images, and related videos, then connects this evidence to relevant source moments. The output is an interactive HTML report for understanding, verification, and practical application. We implement skill-based reference workflow with specialized media readers, anchor-conditioned research, evidence verification, and interactive rendering. Evaluating this task is difficult because an open-ended report has no unique reference answer. Valid reports may use different organizations and source sets (Du et al., 2026a; Sharma et al., 2025; Zhong et al., 2026). An evaluator must still distinguish citation volume from claim support and assess video grounding, cross-source reasoning, and the rendered artifact (Zhao et al., 2026; Leung et al., 2026; An et al., 2026). We address this challenge with Omni Atomic Rubric Trees (Omni-ARTs). Each tree has three levels beneath the aggregate score: three quality dimensions, 23 shared diagnostic directions, and task-specific atomic binary criteria. The hierarchy preserves comparable upper-level scores while testing the evidence needs of each task. Reliable trees also require sufficiently broad and independently verified evidence base. We therefore propose Audited Rubric Construction (ARC), which collects multimodal evidence, screens candidate criteria, calibrates score behavior, and verifies every fact and criterion through iterative human review. Together, Omni-ARTs and ARC define OmniDR-Bench. Here, Omni denotes research across video, audio, image, and text, while DR denotes Deep Research. OmniDR-Bench contains 50 tasks across 19 subcategories and 6,414 criteria. Experiments compare 18 configurations that pair models with agent harnesses, the execution frameworks that manage planning, context, delegation, and recovery. The strongest system achieves 63.3 on the 0100 rubric scale. Presentation averages 81.8 points, while content and citation average only 45.4 and 47.8 points. Under the shared report template, current agents satisfy presentation requirements more consistently than audited coverage, reasoning, and citation-support criteria. Our contributions are threefold. First, we propose Video-Centered Deep Research Report Generation, extending video deep research from short answers to complete and traceable reports. Second, we propose Omni-ARTs and ARC for fine-grained report evaluation and reliable benchmark construction. Third, we release OmniDR-Bench and reference agent workflow. We analyze models, agent harnesses, skill configurations, video categories, and long-horizon research trajectories.

sections.title: 2.2 AGENT WORKFLOW
sections.content: We package the seven-stage agentic workflow as high-level video-research skill, reusable instruction and tool module. It belongs to suite of thirteen skills and invokes specialized video-reader and doc-reader modules as subagents. The main agent carries the timeline, research anchors, external evidence, cross-source relations, unresolved questions, and report data across stages. This shared state reduces repeated context loading and helps prevent goal drift in long trajectories (Wang et al., 2026). sections.title: 3 OMNIDR-BENCH
sections.content: OmniDR-Bench evaluates open-ended reports with Omni Atomic Rubric Trees, separating videogrounded content, citation support, and interactive presentation. Audited Rubric Construction builds and verifies the evidence and criteria for each tree.

sections.title: 3.1 VIDEO COLLECTION AND QUERY CONSTRUCTION
sections.content: We select four families that reflect common reasons for researching video. Knowledge and viewpoint videos require explanation and verification. Consumer and business videos support comparison and decision making. Physical procedure videos require faithful reconstruction and diagnosis. Creative and digital videos emphasize workflows, tools, and transferable practice. Together, these families test distinct evidence needs and report outcomes. We manually source and download candidate videos from YouTube and Bilibili. Each retained video contains claims, steps, parameters, entities, or open questions that depend on visual or temporal context. The fixed benchmark contains 50 Chinese and English tasks across 19 subcategories, with the full collection and curation protocol documented in Appendix E. The query pool combines general report request with two focused views. The video view proposes research directions around theories, cases, objects, or claims. The user demand view formulates concrete decision, diagnosis, reproduction, or application need. Annotators rewrite selected candidates and require each query to need both the given video and external evidence while remaining answerable from public sources. Figure 3 summarizes the resulting coverage, and Appendix gives the query scoring, acceptance tests, and examples. Each task averages 128 criteria, giving 6,414 fine-grained checks. One report takes roughly 2 hours, so one system requires about 100 agent-hours before repeated grading. The deliberate 50-task scale covers four families and 19 subcategories while keeping the 18-configuration comparison tractable

sections.title: 3.2 OMNI ATOMIC RUBRIC TREES
sections.content: An Omni Atomic Rubric Tree (Omni-ART) has three rubric levels beneath the final aggregate score. The first level contains content, citation, and presentation. The second level contains 23 shared diagnostic directions. The third level contains task-specific criteria under each applicable direction. The Omni scope covers video, audio, image, and text evidence and the relations among them. Its directions therefore assess audiovisual faithfulness, cross-modal reasoning, multimodal source use, claim support, image-text correspondence, and video-time interaction. This hierarchy supports comparison at shared upper levels without prescribing one report structure or source set. Figure 5 in Appendix shows the complete hierarchy, gate assignments, and model or deterministic evaluator types. Each leaf is an atomic binary criterion with an expected outcome, evaluator, and evidence difficulty. Semantic leaves bind to independent fact records; structural leaves bind to executable program or browser checks, making each decision auditable. We propose Audited Rubric Construction (ARC) to build and verify each Omni-ART. Evaluated reports never enter ARC evidence acquisition or criterion generation. This separation matters because evaluated reports can omit valid facts or favor the sources selected by one system. ARC therefore builds an independent fact library before writing any criterion. For each task, isolated agents first produce Video Evidence Map of timestamped audiovisual facts. They independently search webpages, documents, images, and related videos to build Web Evidence Map. This external multimodal search adds visual analogues, demonstrations, primary records, standards, and updated context that text search alone may miss. ARC then connects the two maps through support, contradiction, update, explanation, comparison, and application relations. The resulting fact library makes cross-modal evidence explicit before any rubric leaf is written. Omni-ART scores the submitted report rather than compliance with the reference workflow in Section 2.2. Any internal process can receive credit when its final artifact satisfies the same criteria. The fact library specifies salient research targets; it does not prescribe the reports organization or an identical set of retrieved sources. sections.title: 4.1 EXPERIMENTAL SETUP
sections.content: Implementation details. Each run receives the same video, query, tools, and report contract, with shared interface template specifying the required HTML structure and behavior. Benchmark evidence remains hidden. Agents may inspect the video, search multimodal sources, and test the report in browser. GPT-5.6 Sol judges semantic and visual criteria because it supports multimodal inputs, bilingual instructions, and structured outputs. Deterministic checks, including browser probes, verify observable properties. run succeeds when its final report is recoverable and evaluable. Across the 900 modeltask attempts, 835 reports are evaluable and 65 are unsuccessful or unavailable; 19 of the latter are detected unfilled interface skeletons and are counted as failures. Evaluated systems. We evaluate 18 configurations from the Claude, GPT, Gemini, Qwen, GLM, and Kimi families (Anthropic, 2026c; OpenAI, 2026b; Google DeepMind, 2026; Qwen Team, 2026c; Z.AI, 2026; Moonshot AI, 2026). Claude Code covers twelve configurations, while Codex and OpenClaw each cover GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-5.5, and Qwen3.7-Max. We retain each harnesss native behavior because it is part of the deployed agent system. Reporting protocol. sections.content: Skill ablations. Table 5 and Appendix Table 21 separate atomic skill access from high-level orchestration. The five-level ladder runs from an interface-only baseline to the full video-research skill, with exact capabilities and controls in Appendix F.5. All variants use the same model, harness, iteration limit, timeout, retry policy, and report contract. Actual compute use is determined by the agent under each capability configuration. Adding text web research to source-video processing raises the all-task mean from 31.8 to 45.5 points and success from 73.3% to 100.0%. Multimodal retrieval adds 1.1 points overall: its 5.2-point content gain is partly offset by 5.3-point citation loss, separating access to richer evidence from successful citation integration. Full orchestration adds 7.3 points over all atomic skills and improves 12 of 15 tasks, with paired 95% interval of [3.4, 11.1]. Its largest gain is 20.7 citation points, while content rises by 0.8 points: the workflows clearest benefit is improved citation quality.

sections.title: 5 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Deep research agents. Text agents produce cited reports through long-horizon retrieval and synthesis (Qiao et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025; Du et al., 2026b). Multimodal report agents add visual retrieval and interleaved output (Geng et al., 2025; Shi et al., 2026; Ma et al., 2026), whereas video deep research connects source-video grounding with open-web search (Gao et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026b; Zhang et al., 2026b). The former does not center research on supplied video, and the latter mainly targets short-answer QA. Our task uses the audiovisual timeline as the research backbone and returns cited interactive report enriched with external multimodal evidence. Deep research benchmarks. Long-video and browsing benchmarks test temporally distributed understanding or open-web multi-step QA (Fu et al., 2025; Meng et al., 2026; Liang et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026a). Text report benchmarks assess factuality, completeness, citation quality, and user intent (Du et al., 2026a; Sharma et al., 2025; Zhong et al., 2026). Multimodal, process, and rubric studies further examine visual retrieval, tool use, trajectory errors, report logic, and citation support (Huang et al., 2026; Ye et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026; Wan et al., 2026; Leung et al., 2026). OmniDR-Bench instead jointly evaluates video grounding, multimodal evidence, claim support, and interaction in complete reports.

sections.title: 6 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We introduce Video-Centered Deep Research Report Generation and OmniDR-Bench. Omni-ART and ARC provide fine-grained evaluation grounded in audited multimodal evidence. Across 18 configurations, the best score is 63.3 out of 100, exposing gaps in coverage, cross-modal reasoning, and claim support. Future work targets better audiovisual use, efficiency, reasoning, and citations (Appendix I).

sections.title: AI USE STATEMENT
sections.content: Generative AI assisted with language polishing and writing revision. AI models were also used as evaluated systems and as components of the benchmark evaluator.

sections.title: ETHICS STATEMENT
sections.content: OmniDR-Bench uses public videos and web sources, which raise privacy, copyright, contextual integrity, and representation concerns. We exclude private or unsafe requests and follow applicable source licenses and platform terms. The set is not population representative, and its reports should not replace professional advice. Human verification follows applicable review, consent, and data protection requirements.

sections.content: A.1 RELEASED HYPERPARAMETERS The method uses symbols in its definitions so that the evaluation rule remains separate from one released configuration. Table 6 records the current values used to produce the reported scores. All values are fixed before evaluating the compared systems. A.2 OMNI-ART DIRECTION INVENTORY The evaluator uses fixed direction definitions and instance-specific Omni-ART leaves. Figure 5 gives the complete direction inventory. The evaluator column indicates the check type. is multimodal model judgment. is deterministic verification, including static program rules and browser interaction probes. Figure 5 also distinguishes gate directions from core diagnostics. failed gate zeros its direction. The three high-volume directions use saturation τd, while the remaining core directions aggregate continuously. All content directions are primarily judged with J, except observable structural conditions that can be checked with M. The mixed design reserves model judgments for semantic properties and uses deterministic checks whenever the artifact exposes direct signal. A.3 MODEL-JUDGE PROTOCOL Judge choice. GPT-5.6 Sol can inspect both text and images, which is required for semantic content, citation-support, and visual-presentation criteria. It also supports bilingual instructions and structured outputs over long report contexts. We use the same model and prompt settings for every evaluated system. Decision protocol. The judge receives one atomic binary criterion, its evidence note, and the relevant report material. It returns binary decision, short rationale, and supporting report evidence when available. It runs at temperature zero. Each non-gate model criterion is judged once. Gate criteria are evaluated three times and decided by majority vote because failed gate sets its direction score to zero. criteria evaluate directly observable properties without model judge. Their deterministic checks include browser interaction probes. Interpretation. Fixing the judge improves comparability across systems but does not remove model-specific bias. The human study in Appendix A.5 verifies benchmark facts and criteria rather than every automatic report-level decision. The separate study in Appendix A.6 measures agreement between automatic and human rubric decisions on generated reports. Scores should therefore be interpreted under the released judge, prompts, and evaluator version.

sections.title: B TASK TAXONOMY AND COLLECTION DETAILS
sections.content: B.1 SCENARIO TAXONOMY The taxonomy starts from user needs rather than video genres. It asks why viewer would need research after watching and which audiovisual evidence makes the source video necessary. Table 9 lists the four families, all 19 subcategories, and their typical research needs. The taxonomy covers three recurring user goals. The first is efficient understanding, where the report locates important moments and explains difficult material. The second is verification and extension, where external evidence checks claims and supplies missing context or alternatives. The third is practical application, where the report adapts procedure, recommendation, or decision to concrete need. These goals may coexist within one task. B.2 VIDEO INCLUSION AND EXCLUSION Inclusion criteria. candidate video must contain several researchable claims, entities, procedures, parameters, or unresolved questions. At least one important element must depend on visual, audiovisual, or temporal evidence rather than title or transcript alone. The topic must also have enough public external evidence for verification, comparison, explanation, updating, or application. Boundary tests. Each candidate is checked with the three acceptance tests in Table 10. The tests are applied to the complete video and query pair rather than to the video title alone. For example, the pendant-light task depends on the shown socket, coupling, assembly, and product markings, while its safety assessment requires external standards and product evidence  (Table 25)  . These checks establish video dependence during curation; Table 5 studies capability groups and does not separately quantify the contribution of frames versus transcripts. Exclusion criteria. We reject direct lookups, transcript restatements, queries whose answer is independent of the source video, and cases with insufficient public evidence. We also reject tasks that require private information, create avoidable safety risks, or depend on sources that cannot be stably identified. B.3 FIXED DATA SNAPSHOT The current benchmark contains 50 tasks and 17.1 hours of source-video content. It includes 23 Chinese tasks and 27 English tasks drawn from YouTube and Bilibili. The query set contains 7 general queries, 17 video-view queries, and 26 user-demand queries. The four families are nearbalanced, while subcategory findings remain descriptive because some scenarios have few tasks.

sections.title: C QUERY CONSTRUCTION DETAILS
sections.content: C.1 THREE QUERY FORMS We use three query forms to separate broad video understanding from focused research needs. Their roles and final counts are shown in Table 11. general query requests broad research over the complete source video. video-view query selects one theory, case, claim, object, style, or procedure that is present in the video and asks for wider investigation. user-demand query starts from plausible viewers concrete objective and uses the video as necessary evidence for that objective. The two focused views may share video anchor, but they differ in who defines the research boundary. C.2 CANDIDATE MINING PIPELINE Step 1: audiovisual understanding. The video is probed for duration and language, divided into windows of length Twin when needed, and processed by parallel video readers. Timestamped speech, visible text, events, objects, and uncertain regions are merged into one dense understanding record. This record is the only shared input to the two query miners.

An anchor miner proposes video-view questions from the theories, claims, cases, visual objects, and procedures present in the record. demand miner uses the scenario playbook to propose realistic user-demand questions. The demand miner considers six user roles, namely novice, practitioner, reproducer, decision maker, verifier, and troubleshooter. Step 3: scoring and deduplication. Each miner returns five to ten candidates with rationale and confidence score. Near duplicates within and across views are removed before ranking. The videoview score is (α(v))s(v). Here, α(v) is the fixed weight vector and s(v) contains video centrality, research value, searchability, and distinctness. The user-demand score is (α(u))s(u). Here, α(u) is the fixed weight vector and s(u) contains video necessity, external research need, concreteness, and demand fit. The released vectors are listed in Appendix A.1. Step 4: schema and language checks. The candidates are sorted within each view and written to fixed JSON schema. The output language follows the primary spoken language of the source video. Automated checks verify the required keys, candidate count, score range, ranking order, and language consistency. C.3 MANUAL ACCEPTANCE PROTOCOL Annotators review the highest-ranked candidates against the full audiovisual record and the category-specific demand playbook. video-view query is retained only when it is broad enough to require synthesis, specific enough to remain centered on the source, and supported by searchable external evidence. user-demand query is retained only when three conditions hold together. It must express users own task, depend on details from the given video, and require substantial external research. The strip-the-persona test detects demand queries that only attach user label to generic research topic. Annotators remove the persona phrase and inspect the remainder. If the remainder only asks whether the videos claim is correct, the candidate is reclassified or rejected. If it still describes concrete action, decision, diagnosis, or reproduction problem, it remains user-demand query. We reject candidates that merely ask for the next step in the video or request one isolated fact. We also reject search recipes without user need and requests that remain unchanged when the source video is swapped. The final choice balances query quality with language, platform, family, and subcategory coverage. C.4 REPRESENTATIVE QUERY TRANSFORMATIONS Table 12 illustrates the difference among the three forms. The focused examples are translated when the original task is Chinese.

sections.title: D DETAILED AGENT WORKFLOW
sections.content: D.1 ROLES AND SHARED STATE The main agent owns the user goal, execution order, shared evidence state, report assembly, and repair decisions. Specialized video-reader and doc-reader agents isolate long audiovisual and document contexts and return structured records. Each record stores its modality, source, date, excerpt, associated research anchor, and verification state. D.2 SEVEN EXECUTION STAGES Stage 1: acquire and inspect the video. The workflow resolves the video source, probes its duration, frame rate, resolution, and audio, analyzes the request, and prepares an execution plan. Stage 2: build the audiovisual timeline. The video is divided into windows of Twin seconds and assigned to parallel video-reader instances. Each reader analyzes visual content and speech, and the main agent merges the results under absolute timestamps. Stage 3: select research anchors. The main agent selects request-relevant claims, entities, procedures, and parameters from the timeline. Each anchor retains its timestamp, transcript evidence, or frame crop and states whether the goal is to explain, compare, verify, update, or apply the video content. Stage 4: research external multimodal evidence. Anchor-specific branches search webpages, images, videos, and documents in parallel. The workflow opens sources beyond snippets, assigns related videos to video-reader, and assigns long or visual documents to doc-reader. Each branch returns evidence records with provenance, excerpts, media, dates, and confidence. Stage 5: connect evidence and synthesize. The workflow relates video and external evidence through support, contradiction, update, explanation, comparison, and application. Corrective and comparative findings require independent support before the main agent converts them into report claims. Stage 6: write data and render the report. The agent incrementally writes the overview, timeline segments, research findings, media, and sources into structured window.DATA object. After schema and asset checks, fixed renderer creates dual-pane report with the source video, timealigned notes, evidence, citations, and clickable timestamps. Stage 7: validate, repair, and deliver. Programmatic checks validate report data, local assets, citations, rendering, and browser interactions. Fresh-context evidence checks reopen cited sources and test whether they support the associated claims. Required-process checks confirm inspection of related videos, use of visual evidence, and verification of key data. The main agent repairs unsupported claims, replaces unreachable evidence, reruns affected checks, and delivers the validated report. D.3 RELEASED BUDGETS The reference configuration uses Bweb and Bvideo for minimum external-source and related-video counts. It uses Bdoc and Banchor for minimum document and per-anchor source counts. Table 6 reports their released values.

sections.content: ARC separates video reading from external retrieval so that neither branch can copy the others framing. The two evidence maps are reconciled only after each branch records its own observations and provenance. Video evidence map. S1a runs without web access and records timestamped speech, visible text, entities, actions, procedures, parameters, and unresolved visual details. Long videos are split into windows of length Twin for parallel audiovisual reading. Every retained video fact has time reference and its origin is marked as video. Web evidence map. S1b has no path to the source video and searches six routes in isolated sessions. The routes cover named entities, primary provenance, concepts and standards, relevant people, analogous cases, and event timelines. Retrieval includes webpages, documents, images, and related videos because visual demonstrations and comparisons may not be recoverable from text alone. Each route records atomic claims, canonical URLs, source type, publication date, and supporting quotation. Discovered entities are fed into later rounds. Collection stops after two consecutive saturated rounds or at the configured round limit. Saturation requires both new relevant claims and new relevant source domains to fall below their thresholds. Reconciliation. S1c merges semantically equivalent statements while retaining alternate wording and provenance. Numerical or factual disagreements are preserved as explicit conflict edges rather than silently resolved. Confidence is assigned by evidence structure. record is verified when it has at least two independent domains or suitable primary source. It is single-source when it has one source, disputed when supported records conflict, and unavailable when no usable source is found. The evidence record is the auditable interface between retrieval and rubric construction. Table 14 shows the information preserved for each atomic claim. These fields ground later Omni-ART criteria in sources, video locations, verification states, relevance labels, and unresolved conflicts. This mapping ensures that the rubric tests both source-video understanding and the use of external multimodal evidence. S3 removes candidates that lack evidence, contain several claims, use subjective language, duplicate another item, admit several interpretations, or fall outside their assigned direction. Difficulty is computed from evidence structure rather than predicted by model. L0 requires one source-video fact, L1 requires external evidence, L2 requires independent verification or conflict handling, and L3 requires composition across distinct facts. Caps prevent high-volume directions from overwhelming the remaining evaluation criteria. The fixed snapshot contains 4,060 content atoms, 1,234 citation atoms, and 1,120 presentation atoms. It contains 2,363 L0, 1,475 L1, 2,167 L2, and 409 L3 atoms. The retained rubrics reference 3,102 task-local fact identifiers, averaging approximately 62 per task. E.4 VALIDATION AT THREE LEVELS AND HUMAN REVIEW Static validation. Sixteen checks cover schema validity, identifiers, direction membership, logic compatibility, evidence binding, gates, and presentation impact. They also test machine-check eligibility, subjective wording, duplicates, direction coverage, and difficulty balance. The remaining checks examine source concentration, empty-report behavior, direction boundaries, and language consistency. Errors must be resolved before release, while warnings require an explicit review decision. The empty-report check runs every deterministic atom against valid but content-free report and rejects criteria that award unsupported credit. Behavioral validation. R1 receives the video but cannot search the web. R2 uses Claude Opus 4.8 under Claude Code with the full tool set and video-research skill. R3 receives compact evidencemap briefs. The same model and harness generate all three reports so that the calibration varies information access rather than the report generator. This is construction-time check of sensitivity to evidence access; report-level agreement with human rubric decisions is evaluated separately in Appendix A.6. Each task must satisfy R1 < R2 < R3 and R3 R1 > δcal, where δcal is the minimum calibration gain. All 50 retained tasks pass both conditions. Each R2 report is also scored three times to test judge stability during calibration. Across tasks, only 0.89% of applicable criteria receive non-unanimous decisions on average. This repeated scoring is an S5 stability test and is separate from the released evaluation protocol. Human validation. Reviewers inspect the facts and criteria in each assigned candidate package. Each package is independently checked by multiple reviewers in the current validation pool. For each fact and criterion, reviewers mark whether it is correct under the provided source evidence and annotation rules. Majority vote determines each item label, and three-reviewer unanimity measures consistency. Round one records 64.0% item correctness and 77.0% unanimity. S6 uses the resulting package-level error profiles to repair viable packages and exclude high-error packages before the next round. Round two records 87.0% item correctness and 81.0% unanimity on the surviving pool. Its feedback drives the final repair and filtering pass before the snapshot is frozen. Appendix A.5 reports the protocol and results. Issue-driven repair. Fact errors return to evidence acquisition, while criterion errors return to criterion generation or rubric assembly. Each report attempt has 64K-token budget and limit of 500 agent iterations. The process tables use different accounting units: steps count logged trajectory entries, while token totals accumulate usage across model requests, including repeated prompt processing. failed model request may be retried up to 5 times. Each task receives at most 3 complete report attempts, with 10-hour limit for each attempt. If all attempts fail or time out, the task is counted as unsuccessful. run otherwise succeeds only when its final HTML report is recoverable and can be parsed by the evaluator. F.2 STATISTICAL UNCERTAINTY AND SCORE SENSITIVITY We estimate uncertainty by resampling the 50 task identities with replacement for 20,000 bootstrap replicates. All systems are kept paired within each replicate, and failed tasks retain score of zero. The resulting percentile intervals appear in Table 3. For Claude Opus 5 minus GLM-5.3, the paired mean difference is 1.3 points and its 95% confidence interval is [4.0, 5.6]. The interval includes zero, so their order should be interpreted as point-estimate ranking rather than reliable separation. Table 15 reaggregates the saved binary criterion decisions under alternative scoring parameters. It changes one parameter group at time and requires no new model judgments. The alternatives retain the same top three systems in the same order. No system moves by more than one rank among all 18 configurations. Absolute scores vary most when the dimension weights or coverage saturation changes, so comparisons should retain the released parameter setting. It is asked to transcribe the complete video, inspect frames and visible text, and emit one checkable claim per JSONL row with an absolute timestamp. It must preserve the videos own wording and uncertainty instead of correcting claims from memory. sections.title: Atomic Evidence Record Contract
sections.content: Emit one JSON object per atomic claim. Include claim, type, origin, video_ref, sources, and conflicts_with. Each source contains canonical URL, source tier, publication date, and verbatim supporting quotation when available. Do not assign identifiers, confidence, difficulty, or relevance because later stages compute or adjudicate them. G.4 RUBRIC AND JUDGE PROMPTS The atom generator receives the task specification and evidence records but no evaluated report. It produces binary criteria that ask one checkable question and bind semantic criteria to fact identifiers. The screening prompt rejects unsupported, compound, subjective, duplicate, ambiguous, or misassigned criteria. At evaluation time, the judge receives one atom, its evidence note, and only the report material needed for that decision. It must return Yes, No, or N/A with short report-grounded rationale and quoted evidence when present. It is instructed not to award credit from parametric knowledge or from evidence absent from the report. and criteria use the same expected polarity and identifier scheme. Model-judged gates use three independent votes.

sections.title: Atomic Rubric Judge Contract
sections.content: Given one binary criterion, its evidence note, and the relevant report material, decide whether the report satisfies the criterion. Return exactly one verdict from Yes, No, or N/A, followed by short report-grounded rationale. Quote the supporting report span when it is present. Do not use parametric knowledge or evidence that does not appear in the submitted report. Preserve the supplied criterion identifier and expected polarity.

The interface aligns the audiovisual timeline with research findings, multimodal media, claim-level citations, and source records. H.1 REPORT ORGANIZATION valid report separates what the source video shows from what external evidence adds. Each timeline section contains an absolute interval, an audiovisual note, and representative media. Research findings cite external sources and state their relation to one or more video moments. Comparisons and corrections retain uncertainty when sources disagree. The interface lets reader move from note to the corresponding video time and from claim to its cited source. Figure 6 shows these elements in one generated report. H.2 COMMON REPORT FAILURES Polished but incomplete. Some reports have strong hierarchy, imagery, and interaction, yet omit most evidence-map facts and comparisons. This pattern motivates separate content and presentation dimensions. Source lists without claim support. Some reports contain many links, but the cited pages do not entail the nearby claims or are never connected to source-video moment. This pattern motivates separate citation count, closure, authority, and support directions. Transcript substitution. Some agents summarize speech and search its keywords without inspecting visible objects, charts, interfaces, motion, or other videos. This pattern can produce plausible report while bypassing the audiovisual evidence that defines the task. Research that never reaches the report. Long trajectories may open useful sources and inspect relevant media, but the final artifact can still omit the resulting facts or relations. This pattern motivates evaluating evidence integration in the delivered report and analyzing process traces separately.

sections.title: I LIMITATIONS AND FUTURE WORK
sections.content: OmniDR-Bench currently covers 50 tasks across 19 subcategories, and future versions can collect more requests directly from users to expand task, scenario, and language coverage. Some evaluation directions reflect capabilities emphasized by the reference skills, although scoring uses only the final report and Table 5 compares several skill subsets. Future work should develop more general and efficient skills, tools, and subagents that transfer across agent frameworks. The current report
